                    }
                },
                "images": {
                    "total_count": "number",
                    "image": {
                        "path":"string",
                        "alt":"string",
                        "last_updated_date":"datetime"
                    }
                }
            }
        },
        "pageId": {  
            "title": "string",  
            "url": "string",  
            "last_updated": "datetime",  
            "contents": {...}
        }
      }
   }
}

With whatever metadata you have available, you can answer at least some questions like the following:

Question Metadata
How many pages are there? page_count
How many pages in each section? section_title
When was each page last updated? last_updated_date
How many headers exist? header_count
What depth are the headers? header_num
How many links exist? link_count
To which pages do the links point? link_count_distinct
How many screenshots and images exist? image_count
Do the screenshots and images have alt text? image_alt_text
Are the screenshots and images up-to-date? last_updated_date
Are there code examples on the page? page_code_fence_count
Does the code run? code_test_results

The answers to these questions, in combination with other, more targeted data collection like the content audit or competitive analysis results, help scope and outline the shape of your large project.

For example, given a large scale deprecation, a new feature launch, or a redesign of the user interface, consider the following to scope your project:

  • How many pages have images that might need to be updated or removed entirely?
  • How many pages include content about the deprecated functionality? How many include UI-based steps that will be changing?
  • How many links do you need to update?
  • When might you want to update existing new pages or add new pages because the current ones are too long or complex?
  • How many pages will need general accuracy updates or rewrites when they’re updated for this project?

The metadata by itself doesn’t offer enough context to help scope the project, but when combined with your documentation research and product research, you can plan the shape of the large-scale project.

Examine customer data

When planning a large scale documentation project, customer data can be a valuable source when making more tactical plans about what content to write and how to write it. To plan the specifics of what you will write, you can gather data sources like the following:

  • Search terms
  • Website traffic, referrer data, and other analytics
  • Community forum questions
  • MCP server interactions
  • AI chatbot conversations
  • GitHub issues and PRs

Depending on your analytics capacity, this data might be available to you in a boilerplate analytics tool like Google Analytics, a dashboard in your content management, a dedicated data analytics tool like Snowflake, Sigma, Tableau, or others. You might also not have access to any of this data.

You can use the data sources available to you to answer specific questions like:

  • Do the search terms used by customers match the terms used in the documentation?
  • Which keywords commonly lead people to the documentation that you’re updating?
  • Do people ask about this functionality when interacting on the community forum or with an AI chatbot?
  • What use cases and challenges do people talk about on the community forum or with an AI chatbot in context of this functionality?
  • Which websites and content types refer people to the documentation?
  • How many unique viewers and views does each page have?
  • Which agent-derived keywords through MCP server interactions generate traffic to the pages in your documentation that you plan to update?

The answers to those questions then inform your plan for the large-scale documentation project:

  • Inform what terms to include in the topics that you plan to write, such as guiding title or header terminology choices.
  • Guide which content to move or not move, based on referral traffic or organic search traffic that might make a URL slug change expensive.
  • Identify pages with strong, existing information scent (popular search destinations) that might need special handling to make sure you don’t affect existing content findability.
  • Prioritize specific use cases or examples to implement in the content.

Each data trail is a trace left by a user that you can use to derive vague usage patterns that you can model and shape as you redesign the content experience with your own updates and changes as part of the large documentation project.

Plan the shape of the work

As you collect and analyze relevant data sources, you can plan the shape of the large documentation project and the end state that you are working toward.

  • With the competitive analysis, you identified different content types to write and navigation structures to implement.
  • As part of the content audit and documentation metadata review, and assessing the documentation-specific data you identified the scope of the pages affected, constraints and opportunities from the team and tooling, and types of changes that need to be made.
  • You reviewed customer data and activity to guide content decisions.

When you know the shape of the work, you can identify what success looks like so that you can evaluate it later. For example, for a deprecation, success might be an easy reference page to send in an email about the deprecation; for a UI redesign, success might be fewer questions than expected about the UI changes in support chats. Take a moment to define a measure of success as part of your plan.

Write a large documentation project (informed by data)

Writing is the stage where using data to inform your process is perhaps the least relevant. You’ve already made a data-informed plan — this step is about delivery. Enter that fugue state and get to writing.

For example, given a large scale deprecation, a new feature launch, or a redesign of the user interface, this is when you start making the changes:

  • Surgical updates to pages that link to others to mention deprecated functionality
  • Sweeping changes to task steps to change the navigation instructions
  • Scaffolds of a new section of the navigation and accompanying new pages to match
  • Meticulous updates to screenshots

As you start drafting and reviewing, you might discover new data that requires additional planning — some previously unidentified scope of the project, or new user requirements that involve updating additional pages and more product research. Writing and planning can be an iterative process, especially for a large project that runs over many weeks.

But keep the data that you collected as part of the planning process close at hand. There are still some opportunities to use that data to inform your writing tasks in a large documentation project.

Guide AI-driven prompts

If you use AI tools as part of your drafting process, whether to draft content, make larger mechanical changes like link slug updates, or create new files that you then author, the data sources that you used as part of planning can be valuable context to guide AI-driven prompts.

  • Use search terms as context for header, introduction, and page title drafting.
  • Use existing, up-to-date pages as reference models for new file creation.
  • Use curated community forum questions, AI chatbot conversations, and GitHub issues as fodder to create a troubleshooting guide.
  • Include product-positioning context and audience details to output relevant code examples based on actual customer use cases.

If your data sources are available with an MCP server, it’s even easier to add relevant context to your drafting, for example with a prompt like:

Use the MCP server to look up support chats that mention an error or bug from the last 60 days and identify the related features. For issues related to the to-be-deprecated functionality, propose troubleshooting sections in order of frequency based on the findings.

Or for automating content updates related to the UI redesign:

Follow the pattern established on this reference page /path/to/human-authored-draft.md to update the other pages in the same section. For guidance about terminology, use the MCP server to look up the terminology list.

If you don’t use AI tools as part of drafting, but you do use AI tools as part of the content review process, you can follow a similar prompt for the deprecated functionality example:

The following pages are new and address the same use case as the to-be-deprecated functionality on these other 3 pages. Review the headers and introductory sentences for each new section for consistency with the search terms that lead users to click on the 3 preexisting pages.

Data is context for AI tools, and the output can be improved with relevant, curated context for your task.

Whenever you plan to use AI with documentation drafting, make sure that you have an established AI strategy for documentation to help ensure responsible, relevant, and accurate usage.

Inform tactical choices

You can also use data to inform tactical choices throughout the writing process. As you draft content, you might encounter judgment calls like how to phrase a heading or whether to put content on a new page or leave it where it is. In those cases, review the data you collected during the planning process to validate your assumptions about the right approach to take.

Decide what to name a feature

For a specific task like determining what to name a feature, it’s straightforward to use data to inform your decision.

Start by gathering information about existing terms. Which terms are in use, how are they used, and how common are they in the industry? Review sources like:

  • Competitor documentation, blogs, and websites
  • Google ngram and Google Trends
  • Documentation site search terms
  • Google Search keywords leading to the documentation and company websites
  • AI agent conversations

After reviewing the data, you can make a decision (or a recommendation, if you don’t have decision-making power).

If you get pushback, you can share the data that you used as backup for your decision. A discussion is also another opportunity to gather data — maybe you’re missing some context about product positioning, business direction, or lack access to a data source that offers a compelling counterargument.

Data is not an impenetrable backstop. Be curious, not defensive, and build connections to gather information and context that can help you do your job better — and help the user succeed with your product.

Other tactical choices that you can inform with data are the readiness to deploy your changes. As part of your plan, you likely prioritized high-value pages to update based on usage. As you continue to write, you can evaluate the progress against your plan and your knowledge of the product development and release process to identify when your work is “done enough” to release.

Advise review decisions

As you finish the drafting process, data also informs how and when you might send out your draft content for review.

Based on your understanding of the organization and product priorities , you might know that content related to this project is high priority and iterative review cycles with smaller drafts will be easier for folks to review (show that you are doing something), rather than one final dedicated review process that takes multiple weeks with fully drafted content.

Data about your output can also help here — consider how many pages you updated, which ones you’re more or less confident about based on your product research , and the different projects taking time from your technical reviewers — to prioritize what content to send for review when.

You can also use data to assist with the actual review process itself, using a style linter like Vale to collect data about the adherence of your content updates with the style guide rules of your documentation site and validate consistency in terminology.

Evaluate large documentation changes

After you publish your large-scale documentation changes, you’ll certainly let out a big sigh of relief. While documentation updates are never completely done, after you release a large set of changes you can evaluate the results.

As part of your plan, you might have defined what success looks like. With a complex and large project, it can be difficult to measure the effectiveness of the changes if you don’t know what the goals of your content, and the project, are. For example:

  • For the UI redesign, measure support chat volume.
  • For the deprecated functionality, measure referrer traffic.
  • For the new feature, measure user engagement.
  • For the reorganized content, measure discoverability improvements

For many changes to existing content, you want to wait several months and compare user activity against a baseline set from before the change, either from the same time of year or not, depending on how much your content and metrics have changed.

Part of the reason for this is that it takes user behavior several months to adjust to change. Especially for evaluating changes that are not tied to a specific date or customer communication, a longer, baseline-driven analysis is more valuable for evaluation than checking analytics a week after the release and using that as your only evaluation metric.

For guidance on how to determine a baseline, refer to the informative posts from Bob Watson, How you can make sense of your site analytics, and You’ve tamed your analytics! Now what?.

The less analytics capacity you have, the less likely you can rely on baseline data (like comparing before and after changes in data points), but you can still perform pointed data collection to evaluate the effectiveness of your content.

If you don’t see any difference in any of your success measures even after a few months, you could wait a little longer, turn to qualitative data sources like UX research to try to get more feedback, or consider whether your success measures are flawed and consider other metrics to review.

Evaluate support chat volume

For the UI redesign, maybe you hope that less than 5% of support cases are navigation questions related to confusion with the new UI.

Customer submissions:

  • Fewer support cases about the navigation questions, and those that do happen include links to the documentation as reference to help assist the customer.
  • More clicked results in the search terms leading to the page about the changed navigation and fewer unsuccessful searches.

One risk of this success metric is that the support team didn’t know about your documentation, and perhaps your documentation introducing folks to the redesigned UI (compared with the previous UI) was not included with the communications sent to customers. So even if support chats are down, your page views might be low and very few support chats actually link to your documentation.

However, you can mitigate this risk. This sort of pattern in the data can be a reminder that often, publishing the documentation isn’t enough. You also need to evangelize the existence of the content internally, and perhaps externally as well. Build partnerships with colleagues in support, customer communications, sales enablement, customer success, and marketing. Help ensure that blog posts about the changes, email communications about the changes, and internal messages about the changes all include reference to your content as the authoritative customer resource.

Another risk about this success metric is that it assumes that one canonical page is responsible for customer success with the new redesign (one explaining the before and after changes), and doesn’t consider the effect of correct or incorrect task steps in specific documentation pages.

Evaluate referrer traffic and user behavior

For the deprecated functionality, maybe your proxy metric for success is a lot of referrer traffic to the main migration guide for the change, indicating that it is shared as a primary resource.

Website analytics:

  • Track referrer data to see if there is organic and email referral traffic to the main migration page.
  • Track user session activity to identify if users are accessing the migration page from content about the deprecated functionality.

However, there are risks with relying on this sort of data as a success metric.

Quantitative data is limited

Quantitative data isn’t universally or consistently collected for all users across all browsers. For example, referrer data is only tracked if someone’s browser settings, and the website they left, allow that to happen.

As a result, you can’t assume that each user_id that you’re tracking in quantitative data like website analytics or search terms is a specific individual, or One person might be using different devices or browser profiles to access information on your site as part of the same information-gathering session, but might look like separate individuals in your quantitative data.

.

Associating unique user IDs with specific users is often a fruitless endeavor (unless your documentation site requires authentication, in which case you trade findability for precise user attribution).

Quantitative data is useful, but limited. Treat quantitative data as a supplemental source, rather than a primary one, due to these limitations.

An alternative metric that might be useful if you have partnered with the folks sending customer communications is evaluating patterns in website traffic to the page and correlating those patterns with email send dates, open rates, and click-through rates (if that is data you have access to).

Evaluate user interaction with use cases

For the new feature, maybe you expect to get a lot of clicks on the example use cases and users copying the code samples included, indicating engagement with the content and likely relevance of the code samples.

Website analytics:

  • Click activity on code samples
  • Page views on example use case pages
  • Referrer traffic to example use case pages

Using website analytics as the sole data source to measure success is risky. You can’t derive user intent from user activity directly. Click activity on code samples means that the code has been copied, but not necessarily that it was useful or even ran without errors.

An alternative, albeit harder to measure, metric is organic shares of the content on social media, community forum, support chats, or internal Slack messages. If someone asks for help with the new functionality, do users (not on the documentation team) share your content? Using organic sharing of your content as a success metric again relies on successful awareness-raising of your content.

If you think you did a good job raising awareness of the content but organic shares and user engagement with the content are both sluggish, correlate the documentation usage with the product usage to contextualize it. Is usage of the new product or functionality similarly sluggish, or is product usage high while documentation visits are low, even for a complex feature that you might expect to require assistance from the documentation?

If none of the possible success metrics indicate success, you might need to go back to the planning phase and consider if the use cases and examples that you chose to represent were accurate with the product positioning and customer challenges.

Redo some data collection by reading blog posts announcing the new functionality and customer questions posted on the support chats, community forum, posed to AI chatbots, and shared on social media, then evaluate if you want to make updates to the documentation content to be more relevant and useful.

Evaluate customer journey improvements

For example, if your project was to reorganize the documentation to support specific customer journeys, such as configuring a data connection, you might look for signs that those specific customers are succeeding on those journeys more quickly than before the documentation change:

Website analytics:

  • Track user session click paths to and through pages related to configuring a data connection to identify if they are shorter and more focused (fewer clicks on unrelated pages in the same session).
  • Track page views to see if they go up for pages about configuring a data connection.
  • Track referrals to see if there are more from organic search traffic.
  • Track search terms to see if there are more clicked results leading users to this page and fewer unsuccessful searches for related terms.

Product telemetry:

  • Measure the time it takes before a new customer configures a data connection after creating a new account.

User research:

  • Test users in the target customer group and determine if they can more quickly configure a data connection

Some risks of evaluating these data points to measure success is that your documentation doesn’t exist in a vacuum. Other, related customer enablement or product design efforts can produce similar trends in the product analytics and user behavior data that your content might not have influenced.

That doesn’t mean that your content wasn’t useful, but limits the success that can be attributed to your content if there are other initiatives complementing your work, like dedicated training courses, blog posts, or UI tweaks to improve the process. Those content initiatives are not a bad thing — the goal of documentation is to support the user’s success with their goals (through your product), and ultimately any improvement is a good thing.

For guidance performing qualitative user research on your documentation changes, see Bob Watson’s posts Tips for conducting documentation research on the cheap and Documentation research requires more curiosity than money.

Quantitative data encodes activity not intent

You can’t use quantitative data alone to understand why someone did something, only to track what they did. You know that someone searched for “list widgets” but you have no context about why they looked for that term. You know that your page about dashboard layouts got 10,000 views last week when it usually only gets 4,000, but you can’t know from the site analytics definitively why that is the case.

Because user activity data can only tell you what, supplement it with qualitative data like user interviews, well-designed surveys, and text-rich interaction sources like AI chatbot conversations or community forum data. However, what qualitative data gains in clarity of user intent, it obscures that through difficulty of analysis.

AI tools can assist with qualitative analysis, but there are tradeoffs. Data analyst Randy Au captures them in his posts:

  • New data analysis can be faster, but MUST be grounded in slowness
  • Unstructured data is still a pain in the butt (but less impossible now)
  • Labeling things by hand when everyone’s trying not to.

Use data to inform a large documentation project

When you use data to inform a large documentation project, you can more effectively plan the amount, complexity, and type of work associated. As you write and review the content, you can inform tactical choices, inform revisions, and add context to AI-powered tools. When you attempt to evaluate the success of your project, the data you gather and analyze can validate the usefulness of your approach.

title: Prepare to write data-informed documentation
summary:
How you can do data-informed documentation depends on your organization. The data sources available to you, tooling, expertise, support, and time all contribute to the available capacity of your organization to do data analysis, and thus to perform data-informed documentation.

Using data to inform every stage of every project of your documentation practice isn’t the right approach for every writer, or for every documentation team. For some writers, projects, or workflows, it might not make sense to add data.

If you don’t have the analytics capacity, investing in a full data-informed documentation practice might not be worth it right now. I say this not to scare you off, but to set you up for success.

Consider this post the prerequisites for doing data-informed documentation.

Evaluate analytics capacity

Before you start practicing data-informed documentation, assess the analytics capacity of your organization.

The 2026 State of the Docs survey from Gitbook revealed that of the 1131 writers polled, 24% of them do not track any metrics at all. Company size also has an effect:

The measurement gap scales with company size. Medium companies (51–300 employees) are the worst at measurement — 32% track nothing, and those who track average just 1.7 metrics. Enterprise companies (301+) are the best with only 18% of teams tracking nothing.

If you’re one of those writers, that’s okay. You might be at a giant company but be one of those 18% with minimal-to-no data collected and no capacity for correlation across data sources. You might be at a tiny company with a robust data analytics workflow but very few documentation processes that let you take advantage of what you collect.

Depending on what kind of products you document, and how you provide your documentation to users, your analytics capacity can also be different. A SaaS software startup publishing docs on a website has access to different data than a large hardware company that publishes docs as PDF-formatted files or printed booklets included with the package.

To evaluate your organization’s analytics capacity, consider your resources:

  • Do you have data?
  • Do you have the tools?
  • Do you have the expertise?
  • Do you have the time?
  • Do you have support?

Do you have data?

If you want to practice data-informed documentation, you need data. What raw materials are you starting with?

The following data sources provide details about customer and user behavior. For example, some data is submitted directly by customers :

  • Support conversations. For example, transcripts of support chats in tools like Intercom or case descriptions and comments in tools like Zendesk or ServiceNow.
  • Search data. For example, search terms used on Google that lead to your documentation site available from Google Search Console or Bing Webmaster Tools, or search terms, result ranks, and clicked result data that you might have available in logs from your documentation site search.
  • Documentation feedback. For example, votes or ratings, comments, or discussions about specific pages, collected by your content management system or a homegrown solution.
  • Community forum questions and answers. For example, questions, comments, and feature requests (and the answers) posted on a community forum such as Discourse, or a chat tool like Discord or Slack.
  • MCP server interactions. For example, keywords used by AI agents to query your documentation on behalf of a user, collected by logging MCP server interactions on the server side.
  • AI chat conversations. For example, questions asked of an AI chatbot that has access to the documentation (through semantic search or retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)), and the generated responses.

Other data is quantitative and collected when users interact with your product or documentation site :

  • Product telemetry data. For example, for a software product, click activity and session behavior for users in your product, collected by tools like Mixpanel, Heap, Pendo, Amplitude, or a homegrown solution.
  • Website analytics. For example, page views, referrer links, session and user IDs, and click activity, such as those collected by tools like Google Analytics or PostHog. If you distribute PDF-formatted files as documentation, determine if you collect download or access metrics for the files.

You might also have access to more ad hoc, qualitative data sources, often acquired through direct research or surveys :

  • User research reports. For example, the results of research conducted about what users do when they get stuck in the product, the ease of navigating the documentation site, the clarity of the printed booklet, or other documentation-relevant research, collected by a qualified user researcher.
  • Customer satisfaction surveys. For example, net promoter score (NPS) surveys that include questions about or are specifically targeted to the documentation content, collected by a third-party survey company.
  • Product reviews. For example, standardized product reviews that might mention documentation, such as those collected by G2 reviews.

Other sources provide details about your documentation, including how your documentation team is working :

  • Content metadata. For example: last updated date, creation date, title, category, topic length, published version history, and more, collected by your content management system or git.
  • Documentation content. For example, the content of each topic, including the markup for each piece of content, collected by your content management system or git.
  • Ticket tracking data. For example, titles, descriptions, and metadata like closed date, created date, issue type, labels, affected customers, and more, collected by a ticket tracking tool like Jira, Linear, or Zendesk.

The existence of the data is only part of the picture — you also need to evaluate if and how you can access it.

Do you have the tools?

To most efficiently and effectively build a data-informed documentation practice, the data needs to be available in tools that make it easy to access, analyze, and correlate data sources. Consider the following:

  • What tools store the different data sources?
  • Do you have a data analytics tool?
  • Can you use that tool to easily process the data?
  • Is the data in the tool accessible to AI agents, such as through an MCP server?

For example, many documentation-relevant data sources have their own data analysis views, like pre-built reports in Google Analytics or Mixpanel, already-aggregated page feedback and search term data available in a content management system, keyword search term data in Google Search Console, or tables and charts of analytics from your website hosting server.

Without effective data analysis tools, you can easily end up in a nightmare of exported, ad hoc Google Sheet-driven analysis. That can be sufficient for point-in-time analysis, answering a specific question at a specific time, but if you want to increase the analytics capacity of your data-informed practice, you need more effective tools:

  • If you have a data analytics team, identify if they use a cloud data platform like Snowflake, Databricks, BigQuery, or Redshift to collect and analyze data.
  • Determine if you have access to a business intelligence tool that makes performing data analysis simpler for non-specialists, such as Sigma, Looker, Tableau, PowerBI, or others.

Do you have the expertise?

The existence of data and tooling isn’t enough to practice data-informed documentation effectively. You also need the expertise available to analyze the data and effectively apply it to your work.

Consider the following:

  • Do you know how to perform data analysis?
  • What types of analysis have you performed before?
  • Do you have access to a data engineer (or team) that can help collect and model data?
  • Do you have access to a data analyst (or team) that can help design and perform analysis?
  • Do you have access to mentors, training courses, books, or other resources to help you learn data analysis skills?

In addition to considering your level of expertise (and that of your organization) in preparation for data-informed documentation, consider your time.

Do you have the time?

If you don’t have the time to practice data-informed documentation, access to data, tools, and sufficient expertise doesn’t matter.

Consider the following:

  • Do you have time to do anything besides write?
  • What kind of time do you have available for data tasks?
  • Do you have time to try data-informed documentation on one or more projects?
  • Do you have time to teach your colleagues about what you’ve learned?

Do you have support?

Just like with time, if you don’t have organizational support to practice data-informed documentation, the other factors are irrelevant.

Consider the following:

  • How likely is your manager, director, or higher-level leadership to invest in data access for a technical writer? What about tooling and training?
  • Is your leadership likely to support a time investment focused on delivering data-informed documentation, or more likely to wish that you’d spend your time elsewhere?
  • What metrics does your organization track, if any?
  • How data-literate is your management chain?
  • Are you frequently asked for a single metric that can be used to measure the success of documentation?

After considering your access to data and tooling, the existing expertise of yourself and your organization, the available time and support, you can identify the overall analytics capacity of your organization.

Identify your analytics capacity

Based on your evaluation of your current resources, identify the overall analytics capacity of your organization. I’ve defined the different levels of analytics capacity as follows:

None

Basic

Growing

Defined

Mature

Mythic

No analytics capacity

Your organization collects no data at all, or what data exists is not reviewed or used in any way.

Data might be collected by your marketing team, and not available or shared with the documentation team. It might even exist in a tool that you can access, but can’t be exported and is pre-aggregated and can’t be easily interpreted or correlated.

As far as expertise, you don’t know how to effectively perform data analysis, and you don’t have the support to learn. If your organization employs any data analysts, they’re all too busy to work on documentation-relevant data tasks.

Overall, you don’t have time to do anything except research and write documentation. Getting even a few hours to try using data to inform a small project isn’t something you can prioritize. Maybe you’re an overburdened lone writer just trying to keep up with product releases and falling behind every minute.

You don’t have the bandwidth to review or make use of data, if you are collecting any. You simply don’t have the resources.

At this level, other process improvements might be higher impact or higher priority than adding data or practicing data-informed documentation. More information isn’t the problem. Instead, you might focus on updating the release process to include clear documentation requirements and time allotments, or enabling internal and external stakeholders to contribute to the documentation so that you are not working alone.

To start building basic analytics capacity, see my post Where to start with analytics for documentation or Bob Watson’s post How you can make sense of your site analytics.

Basic analytics capacity

Your organization collects basic site analytics data, such as page views and time on page, but doesn’t know how (or does not care) to use them to affect the documentation process.

Maybe your managers look at the data, but they’re only used as observability metrics to make sure that the site is up, or tracked as part of the company web properties overall. You haven’t built any custom views or explorations in Google Analytics, or poked around in Google Search Console.

Other data that you can access is whatever is available in the dashboard of your content management system — top 10 search terms of the last 30 days, thumbs up and thumbs down votes or ratings on specific documentation pages and accompanying comments.

Any expertise that you have in data analysis is self-driven training. There is no data team, no budget, and no time for official training. You’re comfortable looking at dashboards and reviewing trends, but that’s about it.

You take about an hour or two a quarter to make sure the data looks right and there aren’t any surprises, if that, but that’s about it. For the most part, you have some data, some tools, and minimal expertise, but you’re not really sure what to do with it.

If your organization is at this level, follow the guidance in my post Where to start with analytics for documentation or Bob Watson’s post How you can make sense of your site analytics before you try practicing data-informed documentation with quantitative data sources.

Growing analytics capacity

Your organization collects quantitative site analytics data and qualitative documentation feedback. You might even correlate the site analytics data with feedback to identify high traffic pages receiving negative feedback.

At this level, you have access to your data, you’re aware of it, and you look at it.

However, your tooling might be limited to ad hoc data exports that you manipulate in Google Sheets with some basic formulas.

As far as expertise, maybe you have done some data analysis before, or someone else that you work with, but nothing complex. Building a data engineering pipeline or a semantic model with documentation-relevant data sources is beyond your capacity.

You have some time to work with analytics data too. Perhaps some dedicated time each week, or each month, to review specific documentation metrics and take action, like a triage rotation where you review page quality feedback for actionable improvements.

If you have growing analytics capacity, review the different data-informed projects and pick one that makes sense to try. Maybe you have access to detailed search term details, or have been wanting to dig in to the mysterious depths of MCP server usage logs, so you use data to inform a small-sized project to improve the findability of a recently updated page about a core feature.

Defined analytics capacity

Your organization collects feedback metrics, possibly performs correlation with site analytics data, and also tracks business metrics relevant to documentation, like support chats closed with references to documentation or AI chatbot-driven support chat resolution.

In terms of data sources, you take advantage of the data that you get from site analytics tools and your content management system, and you seek out additional data sources across the company and through direct user research sessions.

Your data analysis tooling likely includes a modern data stack, like a cloud data warehouse to store and analyze data. You might even have access to a dedicated business intelligence tool for data analysis and modeling without needing to write SQL.

At this level, your organization likely employs a data engineer and/or analyst, and either you or a colleague have enough data analysis expertise to build charts and evaluate baselines for various documentation metrics.

You have dedicated time each week or month to review correlations between product releases and metrics for the supporting documentation pages, in addition to reviewing and processing documentation feedback data. You review search term trends in Google Search Console and your documentation site.

If your organization is at this level, you might be asked to define metric-based key performance indicators (KPIs) for your documentation. Your leadership is likely data literate, and you probably are too!

If you have defined analytics capacity, plan to apply data-informed documentation to your next medium and large projects that make sense. It might be easiest to start with a large project (counterintuitively) due to the intensive planning often involved with a large project like a content restructure or product deprecation.

Mature analytics capacity

At this level, you have access to multiple types of documentation-relevant data. Beyond what you get from website analytics and your content management system, you have access to product telemetry data, customer reviews, support chat transcripts, AI-powered conversations with an MCP server and a chatbot.

You have a robust data engineering pipeline, and probably a team managing it for you, along with effective tooling and modeling to make sense of the different data sources. On your own or with the support of a data analysis team, you can perform complex analyses like support case deflection and model user lifecycle activity across the product and documentation.

Each week, you have dedicated time to review unresolved AI chatbot conversations for documentation update opportunities, or have built out dedicated automation to do that reporting and categorization for you.

At this level, your data practice is fully developed. You’ve been instrumenting, monitoring, and analyzing different aspects of a well-defined customer journey for a long time.

With a mature analytics capacity level, you might even be done innovating on the product and instead innovating on the process to deliver product updates as efficiently as possible.

If your organization is at this level, you might be doing data-informed documentation in some cases already without calling it that. In reviewing the data-informed documentation framework, you might find opportunities to formalize or extend some existing data practices in your documentation processes, or otherwise identify gaps in time commitments or reporting that can help improve customer success with your content.

Mythic analytics capacity

At this mythical level, your organization is able to write the perfect documentation for your users and provide exactly what they need. Your site displays only the relevant information to them based on the product configuration that they pay for.

You have access to every data source you can imagine, and probably some that don’t even exist yet. Your tooling is agent-driven automation that runs itself.

You have infinite resources to design and run analyses about anything you can imagine. You actually have someone on the team whose entire job it is to apply data to documentation-relevant challenges and do documentation analytics.

At this level, the only documentation feedback you receive from your customers is requests for more examples.

Grow your analytics capacity

After you identify the analytics capacity of your organization, start practicing data-informed documentation from where you are.

Whatever your current capacity, consider whether increasing your capacity or practicing data-informed documentation helps address your ultimate goal: Help customers successfully use the product.

If you have other priorities that can help you reach that goal more quickly, or with higher impact, then do those first.

This framework can offer you something no matter what analytics capacity your organization has: A guide as you mature your documentation processes, or incentive to collect different data sources.

You don't need to measure everything

Despite this being a post about preparing to practice data-informed documentation, I want to be extremely clear that the path to increased analytics capacity is not infinite data collection. It’s sometimes not worth the trouble to measure certain things.

In a post from quantitative user researcher Randy Au, Sometimes, stuff’s not worth measuring, he has some points very relevant to those of us doing more amateur analysis with limited data:

Seasoned researchers know that they’re making a complex trade between the richness of data being collected, the overall cost to do the data collection, the time needed to complete the work, the extent and confidence that results could be stated, the availability of willing study subjects, the technical feasibility of the data collection, the reliability and repeatability of the data collection. That’s not even a complete list, and on top of it all there’s potentially ethical, social, legal, and political concerns related to collecting data and doing the research.

If you have no analytics capacity, or very basic capacity, focus on starting somewhere relevant. Documentation feedback is an excellent example here. If you don’t have the time, or a plan or process to triage and act on documentation feedback, is it worth it to collect it at all?

The data isn’t everything. You can still write good documentation without data. You can still write bad documentation with tons of data.

We all have limited resources — focus your time and effort where it counts.

It’s also worth noting that as your organization grows its analytics capacity, such as by collecting more data sources, your starting level of expertise might not keep pace. Keep in mind your own professional development and seek out continued education, mentorship, or advocate for hiring a dedicated data analyst to help you continue delivering a high-quality data-informed documentation practice.

Start practicing data-informed documentation

If you’re ready to start practicing data-informed documentation, pick a project:

Large project

For example, refocus a documentation set to split the content by audience and create an administrator guide, deprecate a major feature, or update dozens of pages for a UI redesign.

Medium project

For example, write content about a new interactive workflow to review and assign tickets to specific users, or a new type of widget that you can add to a dashboard.

Small project

For example, add a note that data displayed on a dashboard can have latency of up to 3 days, or update the privileges required to turn on a setting.

title: Practicing data-informed documentation
summary:
It’s alluring to use data to drive every sort of decision and action. When you write content for the web, you can gather all kinds of data about your website traffic. Why not put those metrics to work for you?

The content marketing industry is experienced at using data to guide content development, but documentation isn’t marketing. While documentation can drive qualified leads and be helpful to prospective and existing customers, the ultimate goal is to support users in solving their problems, guiding them through using the product, and validating expectations about how the product should work.

As a result, measuring the success of documentation looks less like calculating the number of qualified leads generated and form fills received based on a specific campaign, and looks more like attempting to quantify usefulness, helpfulness, and quality.

Those metrics can be too muddy to measure, but that doesn’t mean that data can’t be involved in the documentation process. Instead, data can play a critical role in planning, writing, and evaluating your technical documentation. I like to call it “data-informed documentation”.

What is data-informed documentation?

Data-informed documentation is the practice of using data to supplement and guide key steps in the documentation process, namely:

  • Planning and prioritizing what content to write
  • Writing, reviewing, and revising content
  • Evaluating the usefulness and quality of content

Data-informed, not data-driven

I’m intentionally framing this practice as data-informed rather than data-driven. Instead of the data driving our actions, it can inform them. Data is context, not expertise. As technical writers, we have valuable expertise in the product, documentation set, and the audience(s) for whom we are writing.

Use data as an enhancement, not a replacement. If you use AI tools as part of your writing process, specific data sources can quite literally inform the context of your work.

No matter how you craft your content, use your expertise to define the path and the data to help light the way.

Why do data-informed documentation?

There are always competing priorities for a technical writer.

  • Product development steamrolls ahead, delivering new functionality that needs to be documented.
  • Customers are contacting support about functionality that launched 2 years ago and hasn’t been updated since, but still gets a lot of use.
  • Sales is selling effectively, but customer retention isn’t as high as leadership would like.
  • Engineers keep shipping updates to the API spec without telling you.

The tasks pile up: new feature documentation, important updates to existing content, tutorials to onboard new users, automated review workflows to improve the quality of engineering-driven content.

It’s easy to be overwhelmed by competing priorities or afflicted by the curse of knowledge. When you’re confronting the uncertainty that pervades the documentation practice, data can help reduce that uncertainty to something more manageable.

How to do data-informed documentation

Given how fast-paced a technical documentation practice can be, what does data-informed documentation look like in practice?

Start by assessing the resources available to you and evaluate your data-informed readiness: Prepare to deliver data-informed documentation.

Then, pick a project to work through:

Large project

For example, refocus a documentation set to split the content by audience and create an administrator guide, deprecate a major feature, or update dozens of pages for a UI redesign.

Medium project

For example, write content about a new interactive workflow to review and assign tickets to specific users, or a new type of widget that you can add to a dashboard.

Small project

For example, add a note that data displayed on a dashboard can have latency of up to 3 days, or update the privileges required to turn on a setting.

Make data-informed documentation a practice

As you establish your analytics capacity and start exploring data-informed documentation, consider how to make data-informed documentation a repeatable practice. Build the habits and implement the processes that make practicing data-informed documentation easy:

  • Set up metrics and reporting in an accessible tool.
  • Use data to inform your work when it’s relevant, useful, and available.
  • Automate the reports to appear in Slack or your email.
  • Make your analytics queryable by an AI agent.

The structure of the data, the tooling available to you, and how you can add it to your workflows is what makes a data-informed practice sustainable instead of aspirational.

As Sarah Deaton puts it in her post, Docs metrics and the stories we tell ourselves:

the real work isn’t finding the one metric that says it all; it’s staying curious, asking better questions, and building a system that gets a little less wrong each day.

Data-informed documentation offers a framework for building that system.

title: API Documentation Writing is not Technical Writing
summary:
It’s not the similarities that matter. It’s the differences.

By Robert Delwood, a Lead API Documentation Writer™

I don’t consider API documentation writing to be technical writing. I know many disagree. I assume they are saying this based on the similarities of the writing styles. It’s not the similarities that matter. It’s the differences.

API Documentation Has a Reliance on the Developer Experience

That doesn’t necessarily mean writing code examples or developing applications, although there is that aspect. It means thinking like a developer.

When a developer reads an API document, the first question is usually not what a parameter means in isolation. The developer wants to know how to use it to accomplish a task. What values does it accept? Is it required? What happens if it is omitted? Does it depend on another parameter?

For example, start with the field name. I consider field names in specific, and JSON bodies in general, to be an extension of the documentation. Names need to be descriptive and specific. My favorite example is maxPltCnt. This conveys no information. Yet everyone on the team had accepted it without question. This includes, of course, the developers, QA, marketing, and perhaps even developer relations. A better name is maximumPalletCount. In a product shipping context, it gives the clients a fighting chance to understand it without having to look it up. This is what I mean when I say to have documentation so good that they don’t have to read it. The writer has every responsibility, if not outright obligation, to push back and get that changed.

So, even describing the maximumPalletCount field as “The maximum number of pallets that can be stacked,” still leaves unanswered questions. Is the default value zero, or is there no limit when the field is omitted? Does the API reject a request that exceeds the maximum, or does it silently reduce the number of pallets? Thinking like a developer means anticipating these questions before they become problems during integration. Too often, new API documentation writers assume the developers know what they’re doing or they automatically empathize with their audience. In many cases, they don’t. The writer is to be that client connection. I’ve said that we’re paid by the company but work for the client.

Developers also think about how individual fields fit into the larger request or response structure. A field might be easy to document on its own but confusing when nested inside several objects. Consider an API that accepts a shipping address containing a countryCode, regionCode, and postalCode. A developer needs to know whether regionCode means a state abbreviation, a province identifier, or a value defined by the API. An easy workaround is just to include an example. “TX”, “MN”, “MA” could answer that question without even reading any sentences.

The developer also needs to know whether the field is required for every country or only for certain countries. A documentation writer who reads the API specification, examines the data structures, and tests a request can discover these dependencies. Without that investigation, the writer might produce an accurate description of each field while leaving developers unable to construct a valid request.

Thinking like a developer also means considering what happens when something goes wrong. Suppose an API requires a date. Many writers simply quality it as ISO 8601. Left at that, it’s vague. ISO 8601 is a general format covering a range of formats. Many may include an example such as 2026–10–23. Better but hardly definative. A developer might reasonably wonder whether a timestamp such as 2026–10–23T14:30:00Z is also accepted. Best is to futher qualify the field format with ISO 8601 Date or DateTime description. Those are defined terms within ISO 8601. Even better yet, also include examples in mulitple formats. At the least, it appeals to readers skimming.

But what if the API rejects that timestamp, what error does it return? Does the API require a date without a time, or does it interpret the time in a particular time zone? These are not merely writing questions; they are questions about how the API behaves.

Data types are another common problem. I’ve seen some OpenAPI specs that classify all numeric values as the data type number. In OpenAPI, a number can be any numeric value. So, why would this be wrong? Exactly because it can be any number. Developers generally classify numeric into integers (whole counting numbers), and number (integer and a decimal number). Because, we’re telling developers what to do, we need to be specific. We don’t want them guessing or spending time finding out for themselves. As instances, the maximum stacking number of pallets for a shipment or the number of children in a school room had better be whole numbers. The cost of a dinner is likely a fraction, $10.99. That, and the developers probably included a specific data type in the code. The OpenAPI needs to reflect this, even to the point of pushing back.

New API documentation writers should become comfortable examining OpenAPI specifications, tracing fields through request and response objects, and testing endpoints when possible. The goal is not to become the application’s developer. It is to understand the API well enough to document what developers need to know before they write their own code.

Developers Don’t Read Documentation

They skim it. They’re using search to find one piece of information. That means they skip over large portions of the document, will not see, much less read, anything before or after what they find. They will not read the guide top to bottom, left to right. If we provide examples so good, they’re not going to even read the field’s text. It’s interesting to understand that we can produce documentation so good that they don’t even have to read it.

API Documentation Is Not Article-Based

Technical writers are used to articles being their main product. This can be broadly characterized by measuring completeness by page or word count, concentration on a single topic, the audience reading sequentially, especially for procedures, and can use previous material to build up or to create a greater context.

Instead, API documentation is field based. The basic unit of OpenAPI is the field. It is a combination block of information of up to 12 tags, typically six. Attention must be paid to each of the tags. That attention is the beginning of thinking like a developer.

Writers focus in the description tag. Clearly, page long articles can’t fit into that space. The information has to be tightly formatted, precise, and accurate. Writing for API documentation means the following.

  • Keep sentences short. This conforms to several requirements at the same time.
  • Short sentences are easier to skim. I like sentence lengths of about ten words.
  • Sentences can standalone as paragraphs. This supports being easier to skim. Mrs. Rayburn, my sixth-grade language arts teacher, would be very displeased with me to hear that.
  • I like the first sentence especially to be short, nothing more than “This field does X.”
  • Sentences should contain only one fact. Avoid combining facts as they get hard to read and increases the chances of being ambiguous. For example, “Set the API timeout to 30 seconds and retry failed requests three times before returning an error.” It’s ambiguous because it does not clarify whether the 30-second timeout applies to each request attempt or to the entire operation, including retries. Being clearer, “Set the timeout for each API request to 30 seconds. Retry failed requests up to three times before returning an error.”
  • For the first sentence, I like “Specifies” to show it’s a request field, and “Indicates”, a response field. Those two words shows them know if it’s a request or response. This acknowledges that a reader can enter the document to any location.
  • Short sentences assist AI readers for that same reason. There’s less chance ambiguity.
  • Put the most important fact first. Put the second most important fact second, and so on.
  • Paragraphs can be any number of sentences as long as they support a single point.
  • It should go without saying but descriptions should be precise.

Repetition

As mentioned earlier, readers search for specific text and so will likely pass over introductions. This means they will miss definitions of first occurrence. For example, it’s common in technical writing the acronyms are spelled out on first occurrence. Another common case is that explanations that apply to two or more cases are included in an overview or a section that applies to all cases. Technical writers don’t like repeating themselves. Those may not be practical in API documentation. I tend to use both the acronym and spell it out in all occurrences, just so they won’t miss them. Depending how lengthy or details a common explanation is, I also tend to repeat those. It adds to the maintenance of the documentation because later changes may need to be made in multiple locations. That may just be a cost of being complete. Remember, you’re here for their convenience, not yours.

The same may be true for tables. Technical writers will want to link to repeated tables. I advocate inlining the tables where they’re needed. Don’t make the readers do more work. They’re there, looking directly at the information they want, so don’t make the click away. It adds to the maintenance but you’re here for their convenience, not yours.

If you do include links, at least always open to a new page, never open it in the same page as they’re on. As way leads unto way in the Internet, it’s always difficult find they way back to the original page.

Furthermore, I never link to third party pages. You don’t have control over them, even if you think they’re the most stable and long-lived pages. In those cases, for example, I may mention in plain text that a date uses the ISO 8601 standard and typically then include an example. After that, I’ll leave it up them to go to that page if they want to.

Changed Files

Fields are likely to be reused in an API. The same parameter, such as clientName or billingAddress, may appear dozens of times throughout the guide. Editing fields is common. For example, a field may be needed to add a format tag of “UUID”. These will affect multiple files. Often, each PR, even for the simplest of edits, may change multiple files. Be aware that managers or PMs unfamiliar with the OpenAPI editing process may be surprised by the number of changes. I’ve been challenged several times as to why the file count was so high. Their implication was not to my benefit either. Be aware that there will always be an education aspect to our jobs. Don’t be afraid of these opportunities.

As mentioned in Repetition earlier, reuse is the Holy Grail in this community. In theory, we should be able to reuse text, from entire fields to simple tables or common phrases. In practice, it’s just not well supported. This is OpenAPI’s weakest structure. Other platforms have marginally better structure.

Unpredictable Scheduling

Estimating writing schedules for API documentation is a problem. It’s not always straightforward to accurately estimate the schedules. There are many issues that can discovered only when actually writing or getting into minute details. This is often caused by additionally nested structures, longer structures than expected, unexpectedly detailed or complex fields, the need to test endpoint exhaustively to understand performance or behavior, reconciling perceived difference in code, documentation, and performance, issues caused by developer oversight, or extensive email conversations. As a rule of thumb, from your initial time estimate, add 50%.

This issue often frustrates managers who are not familiar with API documentation writing. They are used to the smoother and more predictable scheduling of conventional technical writing. As with earlier, be aware that there will always be an education aspect to our jobs. Don’t be afraid of these opportunities.

The Fallacy of Simplicity

Writers must guard against The Fallacy of Simplicity. This occurs when an overly simple example misrepresents the complexity of a real-world operation. Writers new to API documentation often learn from simple OpenAPI examples, such as SmartBear’s Petstore or Redocly’s Museum. And rightly so. That’s what these examples are for. They teach fundamentals without overwhelming the learner.

The trouble begins when writers mistake a teaching example for a model of how things will work at scale. An OpenAPI suite with eight endpoints may demonstrate a technique perfectly well, but that same technique can behave very differently across 300 endpoints or 3,000 fields. As a specification grows, complications emerge that the original example was never designed to address. New writers may come away believing that the simple approach is not merely a starting point, but the only way to do things.

Consider reuse. In a small specification, reusing a field through $ref statements seems straightforward. A field called name might represent a pet’s name or a customer’s name, and its meaning is clear from context. New writers might assume this is, and will always be, the case. But across thousands of fields, name might refer to a company, a medical procedure, a webhook, a destination hotel, or a courier label. Different developers reuse the same term for different purposes, and even fields that describe the same kind of thing can have different requirements or exceptions.

What works neatly in a small example can become ambiguous, inconsistent, or difficult to maintain at scale. The lesson isn’t that simplicity is bad. It’s that mistaking the simplicity of the example for the simplicity of the practice.

title: Issue 57 - How to Tell Your Story
summary:
Your résumé lists what you did. It doesn't explain why it matters or where you're headed. In this issue, you'll build a short story you can say out loud in about 30 seconds that explains who you are, what you offer, and what you're looking to do next.

Have a Better Answer to "Tell Me About Yourself"

"So, tell me about yourself."

It's one of the most common questions you'll face in your career, and one of the hardest to answer well. You hear it in interviews, in promotion conversations, in your first 1:1 with a new manager, and in the hallway at meetups. Most people answer it the same way. They start with their current job and work backward. "Right now I'm at X. Before that, I was at Y..." And the other person's eyes glaze over.

Your résumé lists what you've done, but so does every other candidate's résumé. On paper, you all look equally qualified. Your résumé gets you the interview, but your story explains why your skills matter, how your thinking has evolved to bring you to where you are today, and where you're going next. When you answer with that kind of a story, your listener remembers it long after the conversation ends.

Once you have a story to tell, you can use it everywhere. It works in interviews and networking events, and it also gives you a starting point for your LinkedIn bio, a self-review, or the speaker bio for your next conference talk.

Your story has three parts. Your thread is who you are, your arc is how you've changed over time, and your trajectory is where you're going and why you're ready. Grab a pen or open a notes app, because each part ends with a short writing exercise.

Find your consistent thread

Your thread is the value you bring no matter what job you have. Maybe you're highly organized, or you build strong relationships fast. Maybe you can pick up anything. Your thread is the thing that shows up whether you're writing Go or running a PTA fundraiser.

Your skills are the things you've picked up along the way, and they change all the time. React, Kubernetes, and SQL are skills. Your thread is how you operate, like making messy systems understandable or getting people unstuck, and it'll outlast every framework you ever use. If your thread is "I know React," your story expires the day your team picks a different framework.

"I'm a hard worker" and "I'm passionate about tech" are what everyone says, so they won't help you stand out. A good thread is specific, and it describes something you do. "I turn chaos into processes" tells the listener what to expect when you join their team. So does "I learn the unfamiliar thing fast and teach it to everyone else."

To find your thread, look at what you already do without being asked. Work through these questions to help you find your thread:

  • What do people come to you for, even when it's not your job?
  • What do you do when nobody assigns it?
  • What drains others but energizes you?
  • What compliment do you hear over and over?

If you're not sure, start with the compliment question. If three different managers told you that you ask great questions, you can trust that it's true.

Your thread has to be consistent across your whole life. If you're the one who organizes the team's sprint backlog, you're probably also the one who keeps the family calendar and packs the gear for the camping trip. When you see the same behavior at work and at home, you've found a thread.

So once you have an idea for your thread, test it. Try to point to it in three unrelated places: a job, a different job or school, and something else outside of work. If you can find it in all three, it's your thread. If you can only find it in your current job, you need to keep looking.

Now take two minutes and write one sentence that starts with "I" and a verb. Make sure it holds up in more than one part of your life.

Once you have that, you'll strengthen it by explaining how you got there.

Map your arc

In any good story, the main character changes and grows. That's their arc. Now you have to explain yours.

A list of job titles in order only shows when things happened, like "I was a junior dev, then a mid-level dev, then a senior dev." Compare that to "I used to think my job was to write code. Now I think my job is to solve problems, and code is sometimes the answer." The second example tells you how that person thinks about their work. Your arc should do the same thing.

Characters in stories change because something happens to them that had a profound impact on them, so look for your turning point. It might be a failure or a project that went sideways. A mentor or a manager might have reframed something for you. It might have been a move to a new team or role that gave you a new perspective, or the moment you realized you'd been doing something wrong the whole time. Those are the most believable parts of your story, even if they feel like failures, because they show you can grow from a setback.

Once you've found your turning point, use this template to shape your arc:

I used to [belief or behavior]. Then [turning point]. Now I [new belief or behavior].

You may have more than one of these in your career. Pick the one that best supports where you're going next.

Answer these questions to help you define your arc:

  • What did you believe about your work five years ago that you don't anymore?
  • What can you do now that you couldn't do before?
  • What mistake taught you the most?
  • If you could go back in time, what would you tell yourself on day one of your first job?

Take two minutes and fill in the template. Start with the mistake question if nothing comes to mind. That's a quick way to find a turning point.

Once you've got your arc, you can explain what's next for you and why it's the right move.

Point your story forward

Your thread explains why you're suited to what's next, and your arc explains why you're ready now. Your trajectory names where you're headed. When you tell it well, your next step feels obvious. The listener thinks, "Of course that's next. Look where you've been." Your trajectory gives people a reason to believe in you and what you offer.

That only works if you're specific. "I want to grow as an engineer" and "I want to be a leader someday" don't tell the listener where you're headed. Compare them to this:

I want to own developer experience for an internal platform, because I've spent three years being the person who unblocks everyone else.

Name the problem you want to own or the role you want. Then attach the "because." The "because" is your evidence.

Look for a project where you did the next-level work without the title, or feedback that points toward the new role. Things you built, taught, or led on your own time count too. If you want to be a tech lead, when have you already led? If you want to move into developer education, what have you already taught? If you can't find any evidence, that's useful too. It tells you your next step is to go create some.

These questions will help you find your direction:

  • What problem do you want to own next?
  • What's already pulling you in that direction?
  • What proof do you have today?
  • What's the smallest next step you could take this month?

Take two minutes to name your direction and your evidence. If you only have the direction, write down the evidence you'd need and how you could get it.

Put it together

Now combine your three answers into one short paragraph:

I [thread]. I used to [old], but [turning point], so now I [new]. That's why I'm [next].

Aim for something you can say out loud in about 30 seconds. It'll feel clunky the first time, and that's fine. A draft you can revise beats a blank page.

Here's how it looks for Sam, a hypothetical backend developer:

  • Thread: "I build systems other people can trust."
  • Arc: "I used to measure success by features shipped. Then I was on call for an outage I caused because I wrote code with no tests or alerts. Now I design for failure first."
  • Trajectory: "That's why I'm moving into reliability engineering. I've already led our incident review process and built our alerting playbook."

Sam's thread shows up in the arc, and the trajectory ends with evidence. Anyone who hears this understands why Sam wants a reliability role, and Sam can say it in under a minute. And in an interview, this story can answer some other questions the hiring manager has on their list before they even ask them.

Once you have your story, say it out loud to a friend or a coworker. Then ask them, "What thread did you hear?" If what they heard isn't what you meant, your examples aren't aligned, and you still have work to do.

Keep your story current

You'll tell your story to different people for different reasons, so change what you emphasize based on who's listening. In an interview, emphasize your trajectory so they know why you want this role now. When you're shooting for a promotion, focus on your arc and your evidence. With a new manager, emphasize your thread so they know how to get the best out of you. And at a networking event, keep it short. Share your thread and one line about where you're headed.

Your story will change over time as you grow and face new challenges. Revisit your story every six months or after any big project, especially if you get feedback that changes how you see your work. You should also keep a running list of your wins as they happen. Julia Evans calls this a brag document, and her post includes a template you can start from.

You started with a résumé. Now you have a story. Go tell it to someone.

Things to Explore

  • Video Teleprompter Lite is an iOS app that lets you record videos while displaying the text right on the screen. The front-facing cameras work well on newer phones, so this is a great way to create content on the go while maintaining eye contact with your audience.
  • Paperless-ngx is an open-source document management solution you can use to catalog, search, and manage documents, PDFs, and scans. You can self-host it, and recent versions let you allow LLMs to access your documents. If you want to go paperless but not store your stuff in the cloud, this could be the right solution for you.

Parting Thoughts

Before next month's issue, practice tuning your story for different listeners:

  • Think of two people who'll hear your story in the next few months, like an interviewer and a new manager. Which part of your story should you emphasize for each one? Rewrite your opening sentence for both.
  • Cut your story down to one sentence you could say at a networking event. What did you have to leave out, and does your thread still come through?

As always, thanks for reading.
